meta.title: The Lantau Project
meta.subtitle: 16 weeks, 3 finish lines, ~20,000 metres of climbing

milestones.label: Sea level to the summit of Everest. Twice.

meta.theDealMd:
You are not training to get faster. Your 13 August session ran at roughly **8.6 km/h flat-equivalent**. TransLantau50 requires **6.3 km/h flat-equivalent**. You are already quicker than your race pace.

The entire job is duration. Going from a one-hour ceiling to an eleven-hour day. That means: almost everything easy, almost everything about time on feet, and essentially zero speed work. If a session ever feels fast, you've misread it.

Everything in this plan serves 14 November. RCWT is the dress rehearsal. Suthep is what you get to enjoy afterwards.

**The One Thing:** you don't need to get faster, you need to get longer. Chat Pace. Every week. All the way to Mui Wo.

races.name: RCWT Explorer 30k
races.notesMd:
You have **11 hours** for 30km and 1,540m. You should finish in around **6h30–7h**. There is no cutoff pressure whatsoever, which is exactly why it's the perfect laboratory.

**This is not a race. Repeat it until you believe it.** The purpose is to rehearse TL50 under real conditions three weeks out, and to find out what breaks while it still costs you nothing.

Rehearse everything:
- The exact kit you'll wear at TL50
- Poles, from the start line to the finish line
- The full fuelling plan on the timer — this is your last big gut test
- Race-morning breakfast at the same time you'll eat it on 14 November
- Chat Pace throughout. If you can't hold a conversation, you're going too hard.

**Afterwards, write down three things:** what hurt, what your stomach did, and what you'd change. That list becomes your TL50 fix-list.

checkpoints.name: CP2 Yau Tong, O King Road

races.name: TransLantau50
races.notesMd:
44.5km, 2,508m, 09:00 start, **cutoff 20:00**.

⚠️ **Confirm the official intermediate cutoffs** in the runner's guide before race week. The table above is my pacing plan, not the organiser's limits, and the intermediate ones are what will actually stop you.

**Three things that will decide your day:**

1. **Chi Ma Wan comes early and it's the biggest climb block.** 838m in 12.4km, and you'll be fresh enough to attack it. Don't. Every minute you gain there costs you three at Lo Fu Tau.

2. **You pass through Mui Wo at 26.3km with 18km left.** You will be standing near the finish line, tired, with the two hardest climbs still ahead and 1,081m still to gain. Decide *now* what you're going to do at that checkpoint, because deciding then is how people quit.

3. **Sunset is around 17:40.** If you're on plan you'll be leaving Discovery Bay right as it goes dark. Headtorch on before you need it, not after.

**Fuelling:** 60–75g/hr on the timer, every 20 minutes, no negotiation. When you don't feel like eating is precisely when you must.

races.name: Suthep 20 Day
races.notesMd:
26km, 1,100m, 06:30 start, **cutoff 13:30 (7 hours)**.

- **Headtorch for the start** — sunrise in Chiang Mai is around 06:40, so you'll have 15 minutes of dark.
- **Halfway (~13km) by 09:30** puts you comfortably inside.
- **Target finish: around 12:30**, a full hour of buffer.
- December mornings in Chiang Mai are cool but midday warms up considerably. You'll be finishing in the heat of the day — carry more water than feels necessary for the second half.

Suthep is a *quicker* race than TL50 — 5.3 km/h flat-equivalent versus 6.3, but over 7 hours rather than 11.

Then stop, and go and enjoy Chiang Mai properly.

phases.name: Reboot
phases.blurb: The goal is the habit, not the fitness. You've just put together your most consistent block in six months. Protect that above all else.

phases.name: Building the Engine
phases.blurb: Volume climbs, everything stays easy. Poles come out. The gut goes to school.

phases.name: Going Long
phases.blurb: The hard yards. Two big Saturdays and a recovery week between them. This is where the race gets won or abandoned, and where motivation historically goes to die — which is why the crew and the vertical tally matter now more than in August.

phases.name: Dress Rehearsal
phases.blurb: RCWT. Not a race — a laboratory with a finish line.

phases.name: Sharpen
phases.blurb: RCWT was your last long effort. Three weeks now to absorb it and arrive fresh. Resist the urge to cram — you cannot add fitness in three weeks, but you can absolutely subtract it by trying.

phases.name: Victory Lap
phases.blurb: You'll have TL50 fitness in the bank. The job is to hold it without digging a hole.

weeks.note: 🎯 **Quest of the Week: Recruit Your Crew.** You said other people are what keep you consistent — and right now you have nobody. This is the highest-leverage thing you will do all plan, and it expires. Find one running partner or one group before 6 September. Hong Kong's trail scene is dense; there is no version of this where the people don't exist. Post in a group, ask a colleague, turn up to a club run. Do it this week while motivation is still cheap.

protocols.title: Your Week
protocols.bodyMd:
Three lunchtime sessions, one Saturday long run, two short strength blocks on top. Roughly 4–6 hours, touching 7 in the two peak weeks.

**🪜 The Grind** *(lunchtime, 40–50 min)* — Stairs and hill repeats. Your weekday time slot is too short to build volume but perfect for building vertical, which is exactly what these races need. Climb hard, descend controlled, repeat. Pace is meaningless; effort is everything.

**🐌 The Shuffle** *(lunchtime, 40–50 min)* — Easy aerobic running. Flat or rolling. This is the boring one, and it is the one that builds the engine. It should feel almost embarrassingly easy. Capped at conversational effort, no exceptions.

**⛰️ The Drop** *(lunchtime, 40–50 min)* — Descent work. Find a hill, jog up easy, come down with control and quick feet. This trains the quads to absorb 2,500m of downhill without falling apart at 30km. It is the single most neglected session in trail training and the one that decides your race.

**🥾 The Long One** *(Saturday morning, early)* — The centrepiece. Start at 06:30 or 07:00 to rehearse race-morning logistics, get the fuelling timed, and beat the heat. Trails, poles, full kit, real food.

**🦶 Ankle Church** *(twice weekly, 10 min, on top)* — Ten minutes. Non-negotiable. Miss the Shuffle if you have to; don't miss this.

### Effort, not pace

Hong Kong in September makes pace numbers lie to you. Use the talk test:

- **Chat Pace** — full sentences. This is TL50 race effort. Most of your training lives here.
- **Steady** — short sentences only.
- **Hard** — single words. You'll barely use this.

Your progress metric isn't pace. It's your heart rate coming down for the same effort. Right now you're averaging 147–156bpm for modest work. Watch that drift downward over eight weeks — that's the engine being built.

protocols.title: The Ankle Protocol
protocols.bodyMd:
Your sprain history is the biggest injury risk in this plan. Proprioception degrades with fatigue faster than strength does, which is why rolls happen at hour seven, not hour one — and why a confident descender with weak ankles is more at risk, not less.

Ten minutes, twice a week. Barefoot, next to a wall.

1. **Single-leg balance** — 3 × 30s each leg. Progress: eyes open → eyes closed → on a cushion, eyes closed.
2. **Eccentric heel drops** — 3 × 15 each leg, off a step, lowering slowly.
3. **Banded ankle eversion** — 3 × 15 each side. Targets the peroneals, which are what actually stop a roll.
4. **From Week 6, add: single-leg hop and stick** — 3 × 8 each leg. Land, absorb, freeze for two seconds.

Also: from Week 9, do the last ten minutes of every long run deliberately on technical ground. Rolling an ankle when tired is a trainable skill.

protocols.title: The Gut Protocol
protocols.bodyMd:
You've had GI trouble before, and an 11-hour day in November humidity is exactly the scenario that exposes it. The gut is trainable — but only if you train it.

**Progression:**

| Weeks | Target on long runs |
|---|---|
| 3–4 | 30g carbs/hour |
| 5–6 | 40g/hour |
| 7–8 | 50g/hour |
| 9 onward | 60–75g/hour |

**Rules:**

- **Set a 20-minute timer.** Eat on the beep, not by feel. Hunger is a terrible signal at hour six.
- **Use 2:1 glucose:fructose products.** Two separate absorption pathways means a higher ceiling and less osmotic load — which is often what's behind "gels wreck my stomach."
- **Dilute more than the packet says.** Over-concentrated carbohydrate is the most common cause of the problem you've had.
- **Sodium matters in HK humidity.** 500–800mg per hour. Nausea is often disguised hyponatraemia.
- **Keep a one-line log** after every long run: what you took, what happened. By Week 9 you'll know your own answer better than any general advice.
- **Never introduce anything new on race day.** RCWT is the last day you're allowed to experiment.

protocols.title: The Pole Decision
protocols.bodyMd:
You own poles and rarely use them. That's the worst position, because TL50's rules force the choice at the start line — you either carry them the whole way or you don't have them at all.

Poling is a trained skill and a trained set of muscles. Someone who picks up poles cold for an 11-hour day gets shredded lats, a slower climb rate, and hands too tired to open a gel.

- **Weeks 3 onward** — poles on every single Long One
- **Week 6** — poles on one weekday Grind
- **Week 9** — poles for the full 4h30 recce
- **Week 10** — poles at RCWT, start to finish
- **After RCWT** — decision locked, either way

Given your ankle history and 2,508m of descending, I expect the answer is yes. But test it rather than assume it.

protocols.title: Daily Nutrition
protocols.bodyMd:
Distinct from race fuelling. This is about maximising what you get back from the training.

**The mindset:** you are building from detrained on limited hours. Every session has to produce adaptation, and adaptation is bought with food and sleep. The risk here is under-fuelling, not over-eating — an under-fuelled build is the fastest route to both injury and the motivation crash.

**Protein — 1.6–2.0g per kg of bodyweight, daily.** Spread across four meals at 25–40g each rather than loaded at dinner. This matters more for you than for the average runner: connective tissue adaptation is what protects your ankles, and it's protein-dependent.

**Collagen + vitamin C before ankle work.** 15g of collagen or plain gelatin with 50mg vitamin C, 30–60 minutes before Ankle Church. Evidence is moderate rather than conclusive, but it's cheap, safe, and aimed squarely at your weakest link.

**Carbohydrate around the Long One.** Eat well the day before, and don't run Saturdays fasted while you're building. Fasted long runs are a tool for a different goal than yours.

**Low fibre for 24 hours before every Long One and every race.** This is the single highest-value item in this section given your GI history. High fibre is excellent daily nutrition and a genuine liability at hour six. Most people never connect the two.

**Recovery window.** Carbs plus protein within an hour of finishing the Long One. On the other days it matters much less than the internet suggests.

**Sodium daily, not just on race day.** Hong Kong summer sweat rates are high enough that chronic sodium depletion is a real thing. Salt your food generously through September.

**Rehearse the race breakfast every Saturday.** Two to two-and-a-half hours before the start, 1–2g carbs per kg, low fibre, low fat. By 14 November your stomach should recognise it.

**Caffeine.** Useful, and worth standardising rather than improvising — don't race on a dose you haven't trained with.

**Alcohol.** The night before a Long One is the one to protect. Sleep quality is where the damage is done, not the calories.

**Worth checking:** if fatigue persists disproportionately in September, ask your GP for a ferritin test. Endurance athletes lose iron, and low ferritin feels exactly like being unfit.

**And the biggest lever of all is sleep.** No supplement in this section comes close.

protocols.title: The Commute Protocol
protocols.bodyMd:
Three office days, two hours of bus each — six hours a week of dead time.

Being straight with you: this is **aerobically worthless**. You cannot build endurance sitting down and I'd be making things up if I claimed otherwise. But two of these genuinely target your weak points, and they cost you nothing.

**🪑 Seated tibialis anterior raises — 3 × 25.** Heels planted, lift the toes as high as they'll go, lower slowly. The tib ant controls foot placement on descents and produces that burning shin sensation late in a long downhill. Almost nobody trains it. You have six hours a week.

**🪑 Seated soleus raises — 3 × 25.** Knees bent at 90°, press through the forefoot, heels up. Bent-knee calf raises target the soleus specifically — a major ankle stabiliser and a muscle that takes enormous load in trail running.

**🪑 Banded eversion.** Keep a mini-band in your bag. Same movement as in the ankle protocol, entirely discreet.

**🧍 Standing, if you can get a spot.** A moving bus is legitimately excellent proprioception training — unpredictable multi-directional perturbation, which is exactly what a trail delivers. Loose knees, hand near the rail but not gripping it. This is the best ankle training available on a commute, and it's free.

**🪑 Isometric bracing — 10 × 10s.** Brace the trunk as though about to be poked in the stomach, breathe normally throughout. Modest benefit, but it's genuinely dead time.

Supplementary, not foundational. Don't let it become a reason to skip anything else.

protocols.title: Core & Upper Body — The Poling Engine
protocols.bodyMd:
Twice weekly, ~20 minutes, at home. **Monday and Thursday evenings** work well: they're office days, so you've no trail access at lunch anyway.

Your upper-body goal and your race goal happen to align. Eleven hours on poles loads lats, triceps, shoulders and grip far harder than most people expect, and hands too tired to open a gel at 35km is a real and common failure. So this is training, not just toning.

The relevant core for trail running is **anti-rotation and lateral stability**, not crunches. Nothing in trail running looks like a sit-up; a great deal of it looks like resisting sideways collapse on one leg.

| Exercise | Sets | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Side plank** | 3 × 30–45s each side | The most trail-relevant core exercise there is — resisting lateral collapse is what your trunk does in every single-leg stance |
| **Dead bug** | 3 × 10 each side | Trunk stability with limbs moving independently |
| **Bird dog** | 3 × 10 each side | Adds the posterior chain and hip control |
| **Push-ups** | 3 × (max − 2) | Triceps and shoulders — the pole push-off |
| **Rows** (band or rowing machine) | 3 × 12 | Lats and rear delts — the pole pull. The primary poling muscles |
| **Farmer's carry** | 2 × 40m heavy | Grip and trunk under load. Transfers directly to poles |

Never skip Ankle Church for this. If time is short, do the ankles and three of the six.

protocols.title: The Rowing Machine
protocols.bodyMd:
Dust it off. It's more useful than you'd think — with one hard condition: **it substitutes, it never adds.**

**What it gives you:**

- **Non-impact aerobic volume.** You can add engine without adding impact load while your tissues catch up to your ambitions. That's valuable in exactly your situation.
- **The poling muscles.** Lats, rear delts, triceps, grip — rowing trains the precise musculature you'll need on 2,500m of climbing.
- **Zero friction.** It's in your house. On the days when motivation is the binding constraint, the session you can start in thirty seconds is the only one that happens.
- **It's indoors.** Beats a September lunchtime in Hong Kong.

**What it cannot do:** eccentric quad loading, ankle proprioception, or course specificity. It will not prepare your legs for descending, which is the thing most likely to end your TL50. Treat it as a complement, never a replacement.

**How to use it:**

- **Primary role — the backup Shuffle.** Missed a lunchtime run? 25–30 minutes steady on the rower. Session saved.
- **Optional extra:** one 20-minute easy row on a non-running day, but only in weeks totalling under 5 hours.
- **Never** in Weeks 9, 13 or 16. Those are peak and taper weeks where extra load costs you more than it buys.
- **Technique:** legs → core → arms on the drive, arms → core → legs on the recovery. Keep the stroke rate low (20–24 spm) and the pressure high. High-rate flailing trains nothing.

protocols.title: When It Goes Wrong
protocols.bodyMd:
It will. Here's the triage, decided in advance so you're not deciding it while demotivated:

**Missed a week.** Repeat the week you missed, don't skip ahead. One repeated week costs you almost nothing; one week of trying to catch up costs you three.

**Missed two or more weeks.** Drop back one full week in the plan and rebuild. The long run ladder is the thing to protect; weekday sessions are expendable.

**Something hurts.** Ankle, knee, or Achilles pain that changes how you move is a stop signal, not a push-through signal. Two days off early beats three weeks off later.

**Motivation gone.** This is the failure mode your history actually points to, so treat it as a foreseeable event rather than a personal failing. The response is not willpower — it's lowering the bar until something happens. Do fifteen minutes. Do the Ankle Church and nothing else. Text whoever you recruited in Week 1 and make it their problem. The plan survives bad weeks; it doesn't survive silent ones.

**Behind schedule in October.** If Week 9's 4h30 feels out of reach, TL50 is still on — but run RCWT as a genuine long day rather than a rehearsal, and revise the TL50 target from 10h45 to "make every cutoff and finish."
